name: Do Not Track flag
plain: Reads whether the person turned on Do Not Track.
meaning: A setting few sites honor; LinkedIn says it does not generally respond to it. The collector reads it but excludes it from the hash.

limits.headline: Can see whether you turned on Do Not Track
limits.user_action: Nothing. It is checked when the page or app loads
can: Check your Do Not Track setting
Leave it out of the data used to recognise your browser, in some tools
cannot: Make sites stop tracking you; few honor it
See the setting in Safari, which removed it
Show a permission pop up; there is none
limits.differs: Chrome, Edge and Firefox still have it. Safari removed it.

story.what_it_is: The page reads whether you turned on Do Not Track.

marketing.name: Do Not Track
marketing.pitch: Mozilla describes a browser setting that asks sites not to track you, and notes that sites choose whether to respond.

story.for_you: If it is on, the page sees your request. Most sites do not change anything in response. You see no difference.
story.for_makers: Few makers act on it, and some say so in their privacy policy. It is also a small fingerprint clue, though some collectors leave it out of the ID.

use_cases.example: A privacy focused analytics tool skips counting visits that send the flag.
An ad network ignores the request, since no rule requires it.
A professional network says in its policy that it does not generally respond to it.
A game site reads the flag but keeps tracking play time for ads.
A fingerprinting script reads the flag but leaves it out of the hash since many change it.
A store records the setting for legal notices but keeps its normal cookies.

technical_bounds: No legal weight on its own

linkedin.how: Collector key(s): doNotTrack. Excluded from the hash. Cookie Policy: does not generally respond to DNT.
